Cooking herbs (not spices).Basil: Basil is a member of the mint family, and a classic pairing with tomato; Thai and holy basil taste quite different.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Rosemary: Rosemary is an evergreen Mediterranean shrub whose name means 'dew of the sea' in Latin.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Thyme: Thyme is rich in thymol, an antiseptic used in mouthwash, and has been used since ancient Egyptian times.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Parsley: Parsley is a biennial herb loaded with vitamin K, and it's one of the most widely used herbs in Europe.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Oregano: Oregano's name means 'joy of the mountain' in Greek, and it's the signature herb of Italian and Greek cooking.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Mint: Mint spreads aggressively by runners, and its cooling feel comes from menthol.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Sage: The Latin name Salvia comes from salvere, 'to save', reflecting sage's long reputation as a healing herb.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Dill: Dill's feathery fronds flavor pickles, and the seeds are used as a spice, so the plant gives both an herb and a spice.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Cilantro: Cilantro and coriander are the same plant, and a gene makes it taste like soap to some people.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Chives: Chives are the smallest of the onion family, and their purple flowers are edible.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Tarragon: Tarragon is essential to French cooking, with a subtle anise taste, and appears in bearnaise sauce.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Bay leaf: Bay leaf comes from the laurel tree, and ancient Greeks and Romans crowned winners with its branches.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Cinnamon: Cinnamon is a spice, made from the dried inner bark of a tree, and not a leafy herb.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Black pepper: Black pepper is a spice from dried berries of a vine, and it was once so valuable it was used as currency.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Nutmeg: Nutmeg is a spice, the seed of a tropical tree, and the same tree provides a second spice, mace.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Cumin: Cumin is a spice, the dried seed of a plant in the parsley family.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Ginger: Ginger is a spice taken from an underground rhizome, not from leaves.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Spinach: Spinach is a leafy vegetable, not a herb, and it's eaten in quantity rather than for flavor.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Kale: Kale is a leafy green vegetable, a type of cabbage, and not a culinary herb.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Saffron: Saffron is a spice, made from crocus stigmas, and takes about 150 flowers to make one gram.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Turmeric: Turmeric is a spice made from a root, and it gives curry its yellow color.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Cloves: Cloves are dried flower buds of a tropical tree, so they're a spice rather than an herb.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Paprika: Paprika is a spice ground from dried red peppers, and Hungarian paprika is the most famous.
Cooking herbs (not spices).Vanilla: Vanilla is a spice from the pod of an orchid, and is the world's second most expensive spice after saffron.

Fruits that grow on vines.Watermelon: Watermelons sprawl along the ground on trailing vines, and are about 92 percent water.
Fruits that grow on vines.Cucumber: Cucumbers trail or climb on vines, and they come from India, where they have been grown for thousands of years.
Fruits that grow on vines.Passion fruit: Passion fruit grows on a climbing vine, and its flower inspired the name through Christian symbolism of the Passion.
Fruits that grow on vines.Pumpkin: Pumpkins grow on long sprawling vines, and a champion can weigh well over a ton.
Fruits that grow on vines.Hops: Hops are climbing vines whose flower cones give beer its bitter flavor, and they can grow several meters in a season.
Fruits that grow on vines.Cantaloupe: Cantaloupes ripen on trailing vines, and the netted skin is a sign of maturity.
Fruits that grow on vines.Honeydew: Honeydew melons grow on vines and are best when the rind turns slightly sticky and creamy yellow.
Fruits that grow on vines.Cranberry: Cranberries grow on low trailing vines in bogs, and they're harvested by flooding the fields.
Fruits that grow on vines.Apple: Apples grow on trees, so you won't find them dangling on a vine.
Fruits that grow on vines.Banana: Bananas grow on a giant herb that looks like a tree, with the fruit hanging in bunches called hands.
Fruits that grow on vines.Pineapple: Pineapples grow from the center of a ground-level plant, not on a vine.
Fruits that grow on vines.Cherry: Cherries grow on trees, and the tree often takes years to bear fruit.
Fruits that grow on vines.Peach: Peaches grow on small trees, so they're not vine fruit.
Fruits that grow on vines.Mango: Mangoes grow on big evergreen trees, and are not vine-grown.
Fruits that grow on vines.Coconut: Coconuts grow on tall palms, high above the ground and far from any vine.
Fruits that grow on vines.Orange: Oranges grow on trees, and those evergreen citrus trees are fruit and flower at the same time.
Fruits that grow on vines.Blueberry: Blueberries grow on bushes, which are woody shrubs and not vines.
Fruits that grow on vines.Avocado: Avocados grow on large trees, and they ripen only after being picked.
Fruits that grow on vines.Potato: Potatoes grow underground on a bushy plant, and although the plant sprawls, the tubers aren't fruit on vines.
Fruits that grow on vines.Carrot: Carrots are roots, not fruit, and grow below the soil.
Fruits that grow on vines.Lemon: Lemons grow on small thorny trees, not vines.
Fruits that grow on vines.Pear: Pears grow on trees, and some pear trees live for hundreds of years.

Forms of precipitation.Rain: Rain forms when droplets inside clouds merge until they're heavy enough to fall, and a typical raindrop is only a few millimeters wide.
Forms of precipitation.Snow: No two snowflakes are proven identical, and each has six sides because of how water molecules lock into crystals.
Forms of precipitation.Sleet: Sleet is rain that freezes into small ice pellets as it falls, and in British usage it means a mix of rain and snow.
Forms of precipitation.Hail: Hail forms as ice stones are tossed up and down in thunderstorm updrafts, adding layers like an onion.
Forms of precipitation.Drizzle: Drizzle is rain with droplets smaller than half a millimeter, drifting down from low stratus clouds.
Forms of precipitation.Graupel: Graupel, also called soft hail, is a snowflake coated with frozen cloud droplets, giving it a crumbly, styrofoam-like look.
Forms of precipitation.Freezing rain: Freezing rain falls as liquid and freezes on contact with cold surfaces, and it's one of the most dangerous winter hazards.
Forms of precipitation.Ice pellets: Ice pellets are the American name for sleet, frozen raindrops that bounce when they land.
Forms of precipitation.Snow grains: Snow grains are tiny flat ice crystals, like frozen drizzle, and they fall from low stratus clouds.
Forms of precipitation.Fog: Fog is a cloud at ground level; it hangs in the air rather than falling, so it isn't precipitation.
Forms of precipitation.Dew: Dew condenses on cool surfaces overnight, but it forms right there instead of falling from the sky.
Forms of precipitation.Frost: Frost is ice that forms directly from water vapor on cold surfaces, and doesn't fall like precipitation.
Forms of precipitation.Mist: Mist is tiny suspended droplets, thinner than fog, and doesn't fall as precipitation.
Forms of precipitation.Cloud: Clouds are made of tiny droplets or ice crystals light enough to float, and they only produce precipitation when particles grow heavy.
Forms of precipitation.Humidity: Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air, and being invisible, it's not precipitation.
Forms of precipitation.Steam: Steam is hot water vapor, and the white puff you see above a kettle is actually tiny condensed droplets.
Forms of precipitation.Smog: Smog is smoke and fog mixed with pollution, and is not precipitation.
Forms of precipitation.Haze: Haze is made of dust and pollution scattering light, which is not precipitation.
Forms of precipitation.Rainbow: A rainbow is light bending through raindrops, and the rain makes it but the rainbow itself isn't precipitation.
Forms of precipitation.Lightning: Lightning is an electrical discharge that can be as hot as the surface of the sun, but it isn't precipitation.
Forms of precipitation.Thunder: Thunder is the sound of air heated and expanded by lightning, and it isn't something that falls.
Forms of precipitation.Wind: Wind is moving air, and it can carry precipitation but isn't itself precipitation.
Forms of precipitation.Icicle: An icicle forms as dripping meltwater refreezes, so it's ice, but it doesn't fall from clouds.
Forms of precipitation.Hoarfrost: Hoarfrost is feathery ice that grows on cold surfaces from water vapor, not precipitation.

Bridges in London.Tower Bridge: Often mistaken for London Bridge, this Victorian bascule bridge, opened in 1894, still lifts its roadway for tall ships.
Bridges in London.London Bridge: The current plain concrete bridge dates from 1973, and the previous one was shipped to Arizona, where it stands today.
Bridges in London.Millennium Bridge: The footbridge opened in 2000 and wobbled so much it was closed within days; it was nicknamed the Wobbly Bridge.
Bridges in London.Westminster Bridge: It's the one beside Big Ben, painted green to match the Commons benches, and it inspired a famous Wordsworth sonnet.
Bridges in London.Waterloo Bridge: Called the Ladies' Bridge, because it was largely built by women during World War II when men were at war.
Bridges in London.Blackfriars Bridge: Takes its name from the Dominican friars in black robes who lived nearby, and its station spans the Thames.
Bridges in London.Southwark Bridge: One of the quietest crossings in central London, and the 1819 original was made of cast iron.
Bridges in London.Lambeth Bridge: Its red colour matches the leather seats of the House of Lords, while Westminster Bridge is green for the Commons.
Bridges in London.Hammersmith Bridge: A Victorian suspension bridge in west London, popular with rowing's Boat Race crowds, and repeatedly closed to traffic for repairs.
Bridges in London.Chelsea Bridge: The 1937 suspension bridge, with a golden-hued cable, links Chelsea to Battersea Park.
Bridges in London.Golden Gate: San Francisco's red suspension bridge opened in 1937, and its colour is called international orange.
Bridges in London.Brooklyn Bridge: In 1884, a year after opening, showman P.T. Barnum marched 21 elephants across it to prove it was sturdy.
Bridges in London.Charles Bridge: A medieval stone bridge in Prague, lined with 30 statues, begun in 1357.
Bridges in London.Rialto Bridge: Venice's oldest bridge over the Grand Canal, built of stone in 1591, once the only crossing there.
Bridges in London.Ponte Vecchio: Florence's medieval bridge is still lined with shops, mostly jewellers, above the Arno.
Bridges in London.Pont Neuf: Despite meaning new bridge, it is the oldest standing bridge in Paris, finished in 1607.
Bridges in London.Forth Bridge: Scotland's red cantilever railway bridge from 1890 gave rise to the saying painting the Forth Bridge, for an endless task.
Bridges in London.Tyne Bridge: Newcastle's arch bridge, opened in 1928, was built by Dorman Long, the same firm that later built Sydney Harbour Bridge.
Bridges in London.Severn Bridge: The suspension bridge links England and Wales over the Severn estuary, opened in 1966.
Bridges in London.Øresund Bridge: A bridge-tunnel linking Denmark and Sweden, made famous by the crime drama The Bridge.
Bridges in London.Humber Bridge: Opened in 1981 in northern England, it was the world's longest single-span suspension bridge for 16 years.
Bridges in London.Pont du Gard: A Roman aqueduct bridge in southern France, built without mortar, about 2,000 years ago.
Bridges in London.Stari Most: Mostar's Ottoman arch bridge in Bosnia, destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt in 2004 using original methods.
Bridges in London.Galata Bridge: Istanbul's bridge across the Golden Horn is famed for the fishermen lining its rails and its restaurants below.

Places in Turkey.Istanbul: The only major city on two continents, split by the Bosphorus, and once called Constantinople for over 1,600 years.
Places in Turkey.Ankara: Not Istanbul: Atatürk made this central Anatolian city the capital in 1923, and it is also the home of the Angora cat and goat.
Places in Turkey.Cappadocia: Known for fairy chimneys carved from volcanic rock, with underground cities that once sheltered thousands, and hot-air balloons at dawn.
Places in Turkey.Ephesus: One of the best-preserved ancient cities, home of the Temple of Artemis, a Seven Wonders site, and the Library of Celsus.
Places in Turkey.Pamukkale: Its name means Cotton Castle for the gleaming white travertine terraces formed by calcium-rich hot springs.
Places in Turkey.Antalya: A Mediterranean resort city whose Roman-era Hadrian's Gate still welcomes visitors into the old harbor quarter.
Places in Turkey.Bodrum: Built on ancient Halicarnassus, home of the Mausoleum, one of the Seven Wonders, and a Crusader castle.
Places in Turkey.Izmir: Called Smyrna in antiquity, it's a major Aegean port and one of several cities claiming to be Homer's birthplace.
Places in Turkey.Troy: The legendary city of the Trojan War was excavated in Turkey's northwest, with nine layers of settlement stacked on each other.
Places in Turkey.Hagia Sophia: For almost 1,000 years the world's largest cathedral, it has been a church, mosque, museum and mosque again.
Places in Turkey.Blue Mosque: Its nickname comes from the blue tiles inside, and uniquely among mosques it has six minarets.
Places in Turkey.Gallipoli: The 1915 campaign here shaped the identities of Australia, New Zealand and modern Turkey, and is remembered on ANZAC Day.
Places in Turkey.Mount Ararat: The country's tallest peak, over 5,100 meters, is traditionally linked to the landing site of Noah's Ark.
Places in Turkey.Athens: A trap for Aegean fans: Greece's capital, home of the Parthenon, is not in Turkey.
Places in Turkey.Rhodes: A Greek island, once home of the Colossus, with Turkey's coast lying only a short ferry ride across.
Places in Turkey.Santorini: A Greek volcanic island whose cliffs were shaped by a massive eruption about 3,600 years ago.
Places in Turkey.Sofia: The capital of Bulgaria, one of Europe's oldest capitals, with a long history that goes back thousands of years.
Places in Turkey.Tbilisi: Georgia's capital, famous for its sulfur baths and for balconied houses clinging to the Kura River cliffs.
Places in Turkey.Yerevan: Armenia's capital, built from pink volcanic tuff, claims to be older than Rome; Mount Ararat looms over it yet lies across the border in Turkey.
Places in Turkey.Baku: The capital of Azerbaijan, on the Caspian Sea, home to the Flame Towers and a walled old city.
Places in Turkey.Petra: Jordan's rose-red city carved into sandstone cliffs, built by the Nabataeans and made famous by Indiana Jones.
Places in Turkey.Beirut: Lebanon's capital, nicknamed the Paris of the Middle East, rebuilt many times through its history.
Places in Turkey.Thessaloniki: Greece's second city was founded in 315 BC and named for Alexander the Great's half-sister.
Places in Turkey.Kos: A Greek island and birthplace of Hippocrates, the father of medicine, within sight of the Turkish coast.

Elements with a one-letter symbol.Hydrogen: The lightest element and the most abundant in the universe, it makes up most of the Sun's mass. Its symbol is simply H.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Boron: Its symbol is B. Borax, a boron compound, was mined in Death Valley and hauled out by famous twenty-mule teams.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Carbon: Symbol C. Diamond and pencil graphite are both pure carbon, differing only in how the atoms are arranged.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Nitrogen: Symbol N. It makes up about 78 percent of the air you breathe, yet most living things cannot use it until bacteria convert it.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Oxygen: Symbol O. Plants and algae produce most of it, and it makes up roughly half the mass of Earth's crust, locked in rocks.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Fluorine: Symbol F. It is the most reactive of all elements, so hungry for electrons that it attacks nearly everything, even glass in some forms.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Phosphorus: Symbol P. Discovered in 1669 by an alchemist boiling urine, it glowed in the dark, which is why its name means light-bearer.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Sulfur: Symbol S. The smell of rotten eggs is hydrogen sulfide, but pure sulfur itself is nearly odorless, a yellow crystalline solid.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Potassium: Its symbol K is a trap: it comes from the Latin kalium. Bananas are a famous source, though many foods contain more.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Vanadium: Symbol V. Named after Vanadis, a Norse goddess, it makes steel tough; Henry Ford used vanadium steel in the Model T.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Yttrium: Symbol Y. It is named after Ytterby, a Swedish village that gave four elements their names. It makes red phosphors in old TVs.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Iodine: Symbol I. Table salt is often iodized because shortages of it cause goiter, a swollen thyroid. Iodine vapor is violet.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Tungsten: Its symbol W is a trap, from its German name wolfram. It has the highest melting point of any metal, which suits light bulb filaments.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Uranium: Symbol U. This heavy metal fuels nuclear reactors, and a single pellet the size of a fingertip holds energy comparable to a ton of coal.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Helium: A trap: it needs two letters, He. It is the only element first found in space, detected in the Sun's light before it was found on Earth.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Iron: A trap: its symbol is Fe, from Latin ferrum. Your blood is red because of iron in hemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Neon: A trap: its symbol is Ne. Neon glows reddish-orange; most other colors in neon signs actually come from other gases or coatings.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Calcium: A trap: it is Ca. Your skeleton holds about 99 percent of the body's calcium, and bones constantly trade it with your blood.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Sodium: A trap: its symbol is Na, from the Latin natrium. It reacts violently with water, yet it is half of ordinary table salt.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Chlorine: A trap: two letters, Cl. Used as a weapon in 1915, it is now mostly known for keeping swimming pools clean.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Zinc: A trap: it takes two letters, Zn. Coating steel with it, called galvanizing, protects the steel from rusting.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Gold: A trap: its symbol is Au, from Latin aurum. All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube roughly 22 meters on each side.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Silver: A trap: its symbol is Ag, from Latin argentum, which also gave Argentina its name. It conducts electricity better than any other metal.
Elements with a one-letter symbol.Lead: A trap: its symbol is Pb, from Latin plumbum, which is why plumbers have that name. Ancient Romans piped water through it.

DC Comics villains.Galactus: Galactus is a Marvel cosmic devourer of worlds who first appeared in Fantastic Four in 1966.

DC Comics villains.Mysterio: Mysterio is a Marvel villain who uses illusions and special effects. He's a Spider-Man foe, not DC.

Sesame Street characters.Thomas: Thomas the Tank Engine comes from the British Railway Series books and is not a Sesame Street character.

Gymnastics apparatus.Pommel horse: Its handles are called pommels; it comes from training for mounting real horses, and it's among the hardest events for men.
Gymnastics apparatus.Rings: The rings hang about 5.5 meters high and swing, so holding a cross position needs immense strength.
Gymnastics apparatus.Balance beam: The beam is only 10 cm wide, about the width of a smartphone, and routines last up to 90 seconds.
Gymnastics apparatus.Uneven bars: Once called asymmetric bars, the high and low bars are set about 1.7 m and 2.5 m high; women gymnasts swing between them.
Gymnastics apparatus.Parallel bars: A men's apparatus where gymnasts swing and hold handstands between two bars set equally high.
Gymnastics apparatus.Horizontal bar: The 'high bar' is where gymnasts do release moves like the Tkatchev, letting go, flipping, and catching the bar again.
Gymnastics apparatus.Trampoline: Became an Olympic sport in 2000; invented in the 1930s by George Nissen, who named it after the Spanish trampolin.
Gymnastics apparatus.Ribbon: A rhythmic gymnastics apparatus, a six-meter ribbon on a stick, that must be kept in flowing motion.
Gymnastics apparatus.Hoop: Rhythmic gymnasts rotate, throw and roll the hoop, which is about 80-90 cm across.
Gymnastics apparatus.Clubs: Rhythmic gymnasts juggle two bottle-shaped clubs, catching them without looking.
Gymnastics apparatus.Hurdles: A track-and-field race barrier, not gymnastics gear.
Gymnastics apparatus.Javelin: A throwing spear in athletics, not used in gymnastics.
Gymnastics apparatus.Discus: A disc thrown in athletics, which is nothing to do with gymnastic apparatus.
Gymnastics apparatus.Pole vault: A track event in which athletes use a pole to clear a bar; the pole isn't gymnastics gear.
Gymnastics apparatus.Shot put: A heavy ball thrown in athletics, not gymnastic apparatus.
Gymnastics apparatus.Kettlebell: A cast-iron weight from Russia, popular in fitness, but not used in competition gymnastics.
Gymnastics apparatus.Rowing machine: Gym equipment, not gymnastics apparatus, despite the similar-sounding word 'gym'.
Gymnastics apparatus.Treadmill: A gym machine; a trap since gymnastics happens in a 'gym', but treadmills aren't among the Olympic apparatus.
Gymnastics apparatus.Climbing wall: A sport-climbing feature; the sport joined the Olympics in 2020, separate from gymnastics.
Gymnastics apparatus.Dumbbell: Weight training equipment, not gymnastics apparatus.
Gymnastics apparatus.Punching bag: Boxing and martial arts equipment, not gymnastics.
Gymnastics apparatus.Hammer: A heavy ball on a wire thrown in athletics, not gymnastics.
Gymnastics apparatus.Exercise bike: Fitness machine for the gym, not in artistic or rhythmic gymnastics.

Pool and snooker terms.Cue: The cue's leather tip is chalked often, and a good grip on it matters for accurate spin.
Pool and snooker terms.Break: The opening shot of a game, and in snooker a run of scoring shots, with 147 as the maximum.
Pool and snooker terms.Pocket: A table has six pockets, four in the corners and two in the middle of the long sides.
Pool and snooker terms.Rack: The triangle that gathers the balls tightly before the break shot.
Pool and snooker terms.Chalk: Chalk adds friction to the tip so the cue doesn't slip off the ball and cause a miscue.
Pool and snooker terms.Cushion: The rubber edges of the table make the ball bounce back and keep it from leaving.
Pool and snooker terms.Baulk: In snooker, the baulk is the area behind the line at the end of the table, within which the cue ball starts.
Pool and snooker terms.Eight ball: In this pool game one player takes solids and the other stripes, and the black 8 must be pocketed last.
Pool and snooker terms.Cue ball: The white ball is the only one a player strikes with the cue, and its position makes every shot.
Pool and snooker terms.Masse: An extreme shot where a steep cue makes the ball curve sharply, used to get around other balls.
Pool and snooker terms.Kiss: When two balls just touch, a kiss can send a ball into a pocket, or ruin a shot.
Pool and snooker terms.Scratch: Pocketing the cue ball is a foul, and the opponent usually gets ball in hand.
Pool and snooker terms.Bullseye: The center of a dartboard is worth 50, and it has no place on a pool table.
Pool and snooker terms.Oche: The oche is darts' throwing line, pronounced 'ockey', and there's no such line in pool.
Pool and snooker terms.Birdie: In golf, a birdie is one under par, a bird's flight being a traditional metaphor for great shots.
Pool and snooker terms.Love: In tennis, love means zero, and the word may come from the French l'oeuf, an egg.
Pool and snooker terms.Wicket: A cricket wicket is a target made of stumps and bails, and pool has no stumps at all.
Pool and snooker terms.Puck: The puck is an ice hockey disc, flat and hard, and has nothing to do with the baize.
Pool and snooker terms.Touchdown: A touchdown is a six-point scoring play in American football, not a cue sport.
Pool and snooker terms.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is a basketball move, forcing the ball through the hoop from above.
Pool and snooker terms.Scrum: A rugby scrum is a formation where two packs push against each other, no cue needed.
Pool and snooker terms.Ace: An ace is a tennis serve that the opponent can't touch, and in golf, a hole in one.
Pool and snooker terms.Gutter ball: A gutter ball is bowling's worst roll, where the ball drops into the side channel.
Pool and snooker terms.Checkmate: Checkmate ends a chess game when a king is trapped, not a pool term.

Ships of famous explorers.Santa Maria: Columbus's flagship in 1492 ran aground on Hispaniola on Christmas Day, and her timbers were used to build a fort.
Ships of famous explorers.Victoria: The only one of Magellan's five ships to complete the first circumnavigation, returning to Spain in 1522 under Elcano.
Ships of famous explorers.Endeavour: James Cook's ship carried scientists to observe the 1769 transit of Venus, then charted New Zealand and eastern Australia.
Ships of famous explorers.Golden Hind: Francis Drake sailed it around the world in 1577-80. Queen Elizabeth I knighted him aboard, and it was originally named Pelican.
Ships of famous explorers.HMS Beagle: Charles Darwin sailed aboard this ship from 1831 to 1836, and observations from the voyage shaped his theory of evolution.
Ships of famous explorers.Fram: Fridtjof Nansen's polar ship was built to be squeezed upward by ice, not crushed, and it went farther north and south than any wooden ship.
Ships of famous explorers.Endurance: Shackleton's ship was crushed by pack ice in 1915, yet all 28 men survived. Her wreck was found in 2022 in the Weddell Sea.
Ships of famous explorers.Half Moon: Henry Hudson sailed this Dutch ship in 1609, exploring what is now the Hudson River while looking for a route to Asia.
Ships of famous explorers.Discovery: Robert Falcon Scott's first Antarctic expedition used it from 1901, and it was purpose-built for polar research. She is now preserved in Dundee.
Ships of famous explorers.Terra Nova: Scott's ship on his final Antarctic expedition of 1910-13, on which he and four companions died on the way back from the South Pole.
Ships of famous explorers.Erebus: Franklin's ship in his lost Arctic expedition of 1845 was found in 2014 in Canada's far north, while sister ship Terror was found in 2016.
Ships of famous explorers.Titanic: Trap: a liner, not an exploration vessel. It sank in 1912 on her maiden voyage, and Robert Ballard found the wreck in 1985.
Ships of famous explorers.Bismarck: Trap: this German battleship sank HMS Hood in 1941 and was herself sunk days later. A warship, not an explorer's ship.
Ships of famous explorers.Lusitania: Trap: a British liner torpedoed by a German U-boat in 1915, with a loss of nearly 1,200 lives. Not an explorer's vessel.
Ships of famous explorers.Mary Rose: Trap: Henry VIII's warship sank in 1545 in front of him and was raised from the Solent in 1982. A warship, not an explorer.
Ships of famous explorers.HMS Victory: Trap: Nelson's flagship at Trafalgar in 1805, still in commission in Portsmouth. A naval ship of the line, not an explorer's.
Ships of famous explorers.Cutty Sark: Trap: a famous tea clipper launched in 1869, a speedy cargo carrier now preserved at Greenwich.
Ships of famous explorers.Queen Mary: Trap: this Cunard ocean liner crossed the Atlantic in the 1930s and is now a hotel in Long Beach, California.
Ships of famous explorers.Yamato: Trap: the largest battleship ever built, Japanese, carrying 46 cm guns, and sunk in 1945.
Ships of famous explorers.Vasa: Trap: this Swedish warship sank on her maiden voyage in 1628 and was raised in 1961. Now in a Stockholm museum.
Ships of famous explorers.USS Constitution: Trap: 'Old Ironsides' is a US Navy frigate launched in 1797 and still afloat in Boston.
Ships of famous explorers.Black Pearl: Trap: Captain Jack Sparrow's fictional pirate ship from Pirates of the Caribbean.
Ships of famous explorers.Flying Dutchman: Trap: a legendary ghost ship doomed to sail forever, a sailors' myth rather than a real exploring vessel.
Ships of famous explorers.USS Arizona: Trap: a US battleship sunk at Pearl Harbor in 1941, whose wreck is now a memorial. Not an exploring ship.

Things that hold paper together.Staples: Staples punch through and bend flat behind the pages, a trick that goes back to the 1800s.
Things that hold paper together.Paper clip: A giant steel paper clip statue stands in Sandvika, Norway, honoring Johan Vaaler, often credited with the invention.
Things that hold paper together.Binder clip: Louis Baltzley is credited with inventing it in the early 1900s, reportedly to bind his father's papers.
Things that hold paper together.Glue stick: Henkel launched Pritt, the first glue stick, in 1969, inspired by the twist-up lipstick.
Things that hold paper together.Sticky tape: Clear tape was a Depression-era hit, since people used it to mend things instead of buying new.
Things that hold paper together.Brass fastener: Also called a split pin or Acco fastener, its two prongs fold flat behind the pages.
Things that hold paper together.Ring binder: Friedrich Soennecken patented the ring binder in Germany in 1886, so offices could add and remove pages.
Things that hold paper together.Spiral binding: A spiral binding lets pages turn all the way around, so notebooks lie flat.
Things that hold paper together.Bulldog clip: Named for its strong gripping jaws, like a bulldog's bite, it's a favorite of British offices.
Things that hold paper together.Hole punch: It makes holes so pages can go into binders; it doesn't hold anything together by itself.
Things that hold paper together.Pencil: Pencil lines can be erased, which is why it marks paper but never fastens it.
Things that hold paper together.Eraser: Erasers once were bread crumbs, and they remove marks rather than hold pages.
Things that hold paper together.Ruler: A ruler measures and guides lines, and it fastens nothing.
Things that hold paper together.Highlighter: Highlighters mark important text with fluorescent ink and leave pages loose.
Things that hold paper together.Scissors: Scissors cut paper apart, the opposite of joining.
Things that hold paper together.Letter opener: A letter opener slices envelopes open, undoing what a flap's glue did.
Things that hold paper together.Shredder: Adolf Ehinger reportedly built the first shredder in Germany in 1935, adapting a pasta machine.
Things that hold paper together.Calculator: A calculator crunches numbers on paper and fastens nothing.
Things that hold paper together.Pencil sharpener: A pencil sharpener makes a point, not a bond; the first patent dates to the 1800s.
Things that hold paper together.Protractor: A protractor measures angles in degrees, so it won't hold pages.
Things that hold paper together.Marker: Felt-tip markers write boldly but leave pages unattached.
Things that hold paper together.Compass: A drawing compass makes circles on paper, unlike its navigational namesake.
Things that hold paper together.Ink pad: An ink pad inks a stamp, and it doesn't hold paper together.
Things that hold paper together.Rubber stamp: A rubber stamp marks paper rather than fastening it, even if officials love both.

Things that come on a roll.Toilet paper: Toilet paper on a roll was patented in 1891 by Seth Wheeler, whose design also used perforated sheets.
Things that come on a roll.Paper towel: Paper towels were born in 1907 when a Philadelphia company tried selling thick hygiene paper for school bathrooms.
Things that come on a roll.Sticky tape: Scotch tape was invented in 1930 by Richard Drew of 3M, who wanted a sealable cellophane tape that kept food fresh.
Things that come on a roll.Aluminum foil: Aluminum foil is rolled so thin, around a hundredth of a millimeter, that one household roll covers a lot more than it looks.
Things that come on a roll.Plastic wrap: Plastic wrap began as Saran, which was accidentally discovered when a lab worker could not clean a stubborn film off a flask.
Things that come on a roll.Wrapping paper: Wrapping paper took off in 1917 when two brothers in Kansas City ran out of tissue and sold fancy envelope liners instead.
Things that come on a roll.Trash bags: Trash bags were invented in 1950 in Canada by Harry Wasylyk and Larry Hansen, first for use in hospitals and offices.
Things that come on a roll.Wallpaper: Wallpaper rolls come in standard widths, and the earliest versions in China were hand painted rice paper.
Things that come on a roll.Carpet: Broadloom carpet is woven at widths up to 12 feet and wound onto a huge roll, which is also why it is sold by the yard.
Things that come on a roll.Camera film: A roll of 35mm film holds 24 or 36 frames, and it uses the same perforated format Hollywood adopted for movies.
Things that come on a roll.Parchment paper: Parchment paper is not animal skin: baking paper is coated with silicone, which is why food slides off it.
Things that come on a roll.Raffle tickets: Raffle tickets come in a long perforated roll with matching stubs, so one half is kept by the buyer and one by the draw.
Things that come on a roll.Envelope: Envelopes are cut and glued flat, then sold in boxes or stacks; pre-gummed ones are the reason for the lick.
Things that come on a roll.Sticky notes: Sticky notes come in pads, a product born in 1968 when 3M's Spencer Silver invented a glue that barely stuck.
Things that come on a roll.Facial tissues: Facial tissues come in a box, a product that began as cold cream remover in 1924 before people used it for noses.
Things that come on a roll.Paper plate: Paper plates are sold stacked flat; they were first mass produced in the early 1900s.
Things that come on a roll.Cereal: Cereal is sold in boxes, not rolls; the first flaked cereal came from the Kellogg brothers in 1894 after a cooking accident.
Things that come on a roll.Eggs: Eggs ship in cartons, and the egg carton was invented in 1911 by a Canadian newspaper editor to settle a farmer's argument.
Things that come on a roll.Sugar cubes: Sugar cubes were invented in 1843 by a Czech sugar factory manager after his wife cut her finger on a sugar loaf.
Things that come on a roll.Crayons: Crayons come in boxes, and a box of 64 with a built-in sharpener has been sold since 1958.
Things that come on a roll.Notebook: Notebooks are bound or stitched, though a long scroll is the oldest writing format still used for the Torah.
Things that come on a roll.Batteries: Batteries are sold in blister packs, and the AA size only became standard in the 1950s.
Things that come on a roll.Matches: Matches come in boxes or books, and the modern safety match was invented in Sweden in 1844.
Things that come on a roll.Playing cards: A standard deck has 52 cards, plus jokers, and comes in a box instead of a roll.

Things you can recharge.Laptop: Keeping a laptop's battery between about 20 and 80 percent can help it last longer than constant full charges.
Things you can recharge.Electric toothbrush: Many use inductive charging, with the handle sitting on a base and no exposed metal contacts, which is safe in a wet bathroom.
Things you can recharge.Smartwatch: Smartwatches usually charge through a magnetic puck or contacts on the back.
Things you can recharge.Wireless earbuds: Each bud has a battery as small as a coin, and the case holds extra charge to top them up.
Things you can recharge.Tablet: Tablets have large lithium-polymer batteries, which take up most of their interior.
Things you can recharge.Electric car: Regenerative braking in electric cars converts motion back into stored energy, so slowing down recharges the battery slightly.
Things you can recharge.Cordless drill: Cordless drills went from slow nickel-cadmium batteries to lithium-ion, which are lighter and hold more charge.
Things you can recharge.E-reader: E-ink screens use power only when changing pages, so an e-reader can last weeks on a single charge.
Things you can recharge.Power bank: A power bank is a battery that charges other gadgets, and it must be charged itself.
Things you can recharge.Robot vacuum: Many return to their charging dock on their own when the battery runs low, using infrared signals to find it.
Things you can recharge.Electric scooter: Most use lithium-ion packs, and the range depends heavily on rider weight, hills, and speed.
Things you can recharge.Toaster: A toaster draws mains power and has no battery, so there's nothing to recharge.
Things you can recharge.Kettle: A cordless kettle sits on a base for power, but it doesn't store energy, so there's nothing to recharge.
Things you can recharge.Fridge: A fridge runs on mains power, and when the power stops, it keeps food cold for only a few hours.
Things you can recharge.Microwave: A microwave takes power from the wall, and it has no battery.
Things you can recharge.Candle: Once it burns, wax is gone, so a candle can't be recharged, though the leftover stub can be melted into a new one.
Things you can recharge.Mechanical pencil: A mechanical pencil is refilled with lead, but it can't be recharged.
Things you can recharge.Television: TVs run on mains power, though a few portable models once had rechargeable batteries.
Things you can recharge.Hair dryer: Almost all hair dryers are corded, since they draw more power than a small battery could supply.
Things you can recharge.Washing machine: A washing machine needs mains power and water, and it has no battery, so it can't be recharged.
Things you can recharge.Blender: A blender's motor draws power from the wall, though cordless portable blenders do exist.
Things you can recharge.Dishwasher: A dishwasher is hardwired to the home's power and plumbing, and there's no battery to recharge.
Things you can recharge.Corded drill: The word corded gives it away: it plugs into the wall, unlike its cordless sibling with a rechargeable pack.

Words for a trash can.Bin: 'Bin' is the standard British word for a trash can, and it comes from an Old English word for a basket or manger.
Words for a trash can.Garbage can: 'Garbage can' is the usual American term; New York's Sanitation Department made lidded metal cans mandatory in the 1890s.
Words for a trash can.Wastebasket: A wastebasket is typically the small open container beside a desk, which is why it holds paper more than kitchen scraps.
Words for a trash can.Dustbin: A dustbin got its name from the household dust and ash once thrown in it, back when coal fires were the norm.
Words for a trash can.Litter bin: 'Litter bin' is common in British parks and streets, where fines for dropping litter are called fixed penalty notices.
Words for a trash can.Rubbish bin: 'Rubbish bin' is the Australian and British phrase, and 'rubbish' comes from an Old French word for rubble.
Words for a trash can.Wastepaper basket: A wastepaper basket sounds old fashioned, yet it is still the formal name used in many offices and dictionaries.
Words for a trash can.Garbage pail: 'Garbage pail' is used in some parts of the American Northeast, and gave its name to the Garbage Pail Kids cards of the 1980s.
Words for a trash can.Trash bin: A trash bin is the all-purpose American term, and some city versions come with wheels and a hinged lid.
Words for a trash can.Dustpan: A dustpan collects what you sweep up and then feeds it to the bin, but it isn't itself a bin.
Words for a trash can.Laundry hamper: A laundry hamper holds dirty clothes, so it only stores things destined for the wash, not rubbish.
Words for a trash can.Mailbox: A mailbox is for letters; in the US it is federally protected property, so tampering with one is a crime.
Words for a trash can.Pantry: A pantry stores food, and the word comes from the Latin for bread, panis.
Words for a trash can.Cupboard: A cupboard was originally a board for cups, meaning a table to display cups on.
Words for a trash can.Drawer: A drawer stores things you intend to keep, even if it often becomes a junk drawer.
Words for a trash can.Coffer: A coffer is a strongbox for valuables, the opposite of a place for waste.
Words for a trash can.Hutch: A hutch is a small cabinet or an animal pen, such as a rabbit's, but it isn't for garbage.
Words for a trash can.Locker: A locker keeps your belongings secure, and the name comes from the lock that closes it.
Words for a trash can.Crate: A crate is a packing case, and it can be reused many times rather than thrown out.
Words for a trash can.Bread bin: A bread bin keeps loaves fresh and looks a lot like a bin, but it holds bread, not waste.
Words for a trash can.Toolbox: A toolbox is where tools live, and it's one container you'd never want to throw out.
Words for a trash can.Pencil case: A pencil case stores stationery, and its contents are meant to be kept and used.
Words for a trash can.Hope chest: A hope chest is a trunk where women once stored linens for marriage, a very different kind of keeping.
Words for a trash can.Linen closet: A linen closet stores sheets and towels, and it is one cupboard where nothing is ever thrown away.

Parts of a toilet.Seat: Toilet seats are often shaped as an open-front horseshoe in public restrooms, because it's considered more hygienic to use.
Parts of a toilet.Lid: Flushing with the lid up can spray a fine aerosol of droplets into the air, which is why many experts advise closing it first.
Parts of a toilet.Bowl: Modern bowls use a curved S-shaped trap that keeps a plug of water in place, blocking sewer gas from rising into the room.
Parts of a toilet.Cistern: The word comes from the Latin for a reservoir. Many older cisterns sat high on the wall, so gravity gave the flush its force.
Parts of a toilet.Flush handle: The handle just lifts a chain or lever inside the tank. Dual-flush versions let you pick a small or large flush to save water.
Parts of a toilet.Float ball: This hollow ball rides the water level up and shuts off the incoming supply. It's the same trick used in old steam boilers and livestock troughs.
Parts of a toilet.Flapper: The rubber flapper is the most common culprit for a toilet that runs on. A worn one leaks slowly, so the tank keeps refilling.
Parts of a toilet.Fill valve: Also called a ballcock in older designs, it refills the tank after each flush. Modern ones are quieter and shut off with a float cup.
Parts of a toilet.Wax ring: A humble ring of wax seals the base of the toilet against the floor flange. It works by squishing flat, so it must be replaced if you lift the toilet.
Parts of a toilet.Faucet: A faucet belongs at the sink or bath. The toilet itself has no tap, only a fill valve hidden inside the tank.
Parts of a toilet.Spout: A spout belongs on a faucet or kettle. The toilet fills through a hidden inlet and has no spout at all.
Parts of a toilet.Shower head: Shower heads can harbor bacteria in their nozzles, but they are nowhere near the toilet's plumbing parts.
Parts of a toilet.Towel rail: Heated towel rails are popular in Europe, but this bathroom fixture has nothing to do with how a toilet flushes.
Parts of a toilet.Soap dish: Soap dishes sit by sinks and showers. Toilets rely on water alone, with no soap built in.
Parts of a toilet.Plughole: A plughole sits in the bath or sink and drains by gravity. A toilet drains through a curved trap instead of a plug.
Parts of a toilet.Mirror: Bathroom mirrors are often treated to resist fog, a problem the toilet area never has.
Parts of a toilet.Curtain rod: A curtain rod holds up the shower curtain. The toilet, with its tank and bowl, has no use for one.
Parts of a toilet.Bath mat: Bath mats prevent slips on wet tile and belong beside the tub, not as a working part of the toilet.
Parts of a toilet.Shower tray: A shower tray catches water at your feet and funnels it to a drain. The toilet has its own very different drain trap.
Parts of a toilet.Toothbrush holder: A toothbrush holder is a counter accessory. It isn't a working component of the toilet.
Parts of a toilet.Medicine cabinet: Medicine cabinets hang on the wall for storage. They have no role in how a toilet operates.
Parts of a toilet.Tile grout: Grout fills the gaps between tiles. It's part of the bathroom's surface, not of the toilet fixture itself.
Parts of a toilet.Bath plug: A bath plug stops water draining from the tub. A toilet works the opposite way: its flush is designed to drain fast.
Parts of a toilet.Loofah: Despite its sponge-like look, a loofah is a dried gourd fruit, scrubbed in the shower, not part of any toilet.

Parts of the face.Forehead: The forehead is the part of the face above the eyebrows, and it's the front of the frontal bone.
Parts of the face.Cheek: The cheek has a layer of fat, and it also makes you blush, as blood vessels widen when you're embarrassed.
Parts of the face.Chin: The chin is a feature mostly unique to modern humans, and no other primate has a true one.
Parts of the face.Nose: The nose can detect thousands of odors, and it warms and moistens the air you breathe in.
Parts of the face.Eyebrow: Eyebrows keep sweat and rain out of the eyes, and they also help us show emotion.
Parts of the face.Temple: The temple is the flat area beside the forehead, and the word comes from Latin for the side of the head.
Parts of the face.Jaw: The jaw is the lower part of the face, and it houses the lower teeth.
Parts of the face.Lips: Lips are packed with nerve endings and have no oil glands, which is why they get chapped.
Parts of the face.Eyelid: Eyelids blink around 15 times a minute, and they spread tears across the eye.
Parts of the face.Nostril: Nostrils are the two openings of the nose, and each one leads to a separate passage.
Parts of the face.Eyelash: Eyelashes protect your eyes from dust, and they live only a few months before falling out.
Parts of the face.Nape: The nape is the back of the neck, where hair often grows in a whorl. It sits on the neck, not the face.
Parts of the face.Shoulder: The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, but it sits well below the face, so it's out.
Parts of the face.Collarbone: The collarbone is the most commonly broken bone in the body, and it lies below the neck, far from the face.
Parts of the face.Elbow: The elbow is a hinge joint with the 'funny bone' nerve, and it's nowhere near the face, so it doesn't belong.
Parts of the face.Scalp: The scalp is a trap: it covers the top of the head and carries your hair, yet the face is defined as the front only.
Parts of the face.Armpit: The armpit is called the axilla in anatomy, and it's under the arm, far from the face.
Parts of the face.Navel: The navel marks where the umbilical cord once attached. It's on the belly and not on the face.
Parts of the face.Knee: The knee is the body's largest joint, and it belongs to the leg, not the face.
Parts of the face.Shin: The shin is the front of the lower leg, where the tibia lies just under the skin, so it's no face part.
Parts of the face.Palm: The palm is the inner surface of the hand and has no hair, but it's not a face part.
Parts of the face.Spine: The spine has 33 vertebrae and runs down the back. It begins at the skull, but is not part of the face.
Parts of the face.Heel: The heel is the rear of the foot and takes the first impact when you walk, so it's not on the face.
Parts of the face.Wrist: The wrist has eight small bones in a cluster, and it joins hand and forearm, far from the face.

Common sports injuries.Sprained ankle: One of the most common sports injuries, it's a stretched or torn ligament, and often caused by landing on another player's foot.
Common sports injuries.Torn ACL: The anterior cruciate ligament stabilizes the knee, and tears are especially common in soccer, basketball and skiing.
Common sports injuries.Tennis elbow: Despite the name, most people who get it aren't tennis players; it's overuse of forearm tendons from repetitive gripping.
Common sports injuries.Shin splints: Pain along the shinbone from overtraining, common in runners who increase mileage too quickly.
Common sports injuries.Concussion: A concussion is a brain injury from a blow or jolt, and it needs rest even without losing consciousness.
Common sports injuries.Pulled hamstring: Sprinters often strain the hamstring, the muscle group at the back of the thigh, during an explosive push-off.
Common sports injuries.Dislocated shoulder: The shoulder is the body's most mobile joint, which makes it also the one most likely to dislocate.
Common sports injuries.Rotator cuff tear: Four muscles and tendons stabilize the shoulder, and tears are common in pitchers and swimmers.
Common sports injuries.Stress fracture: A tiny crack in a bone caused by repeated impact, often in the foot or shin of runners and dancers.
Common sports injuries.Runner's knee: A pain around the kneecap, also called patellofemoral pain, that is among the most common running complaints.
Common sports injuries.Groin strain: A pulled inner-thigh muscle, typical in hockey and soccer where quick sideways pushes are common.
Common sports injuries.Turf toe: A sprain at the big toe's base joint, named for hard artificial surfaces, that is common among football players.
Common sports injuries.Golfer's elbow: Tendon pain on the inner elbow, the mirror of tennis elbow, and it affects plenty of non-golfers too.
Common sports injuries.Chickenpox: A trap: chickenpox is a viral infection, so it isn't a sports injury, though it will sideline you from games.
Common sports injuries.Measles: Measles is a highly contagious virus, not an injury, and it can spread fast through a team.
Common sports injuries.Hiccups: Hiccups are diaphragm spasms, a nuisance more than an injury, even if they strike mid-game.
Common sports injuries.Diabetes: Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disease, though plenty of pro athletes compete successfully with it.
Common sports injuries.Flu: Flu is infectious, not an injury, and athletes are advised to rest because training with a fever can strain the heart.
Common sports injuries.Cavity: A cavity is tooth decay, not a sports injury, though sports drinks can contribute to it.
Common sports injuries.Tonsillitis: Tonsillitis is an infection of the throat's tonsils, not something a game causes.
Common sports injuries.Pink eye: Pink eye is an infection or allergy of the eye surface, contagious through touching, not trauma.
Common sports injuries.Common cold: A cold is a virus, not an injury, but it spreads easily in locker rooms.
Common sports injuries.Mumps: Mumps is a viral infection that swells the cheeks, and vaccination has made it rare.
Common sports injuries.Head lice: Lice are tiny insects living on scalps, and they spread by head contact, so wrestling teams do sometimes see them.

Things you shouldn't pet.Porcupine: A porcupine has about 30,000 quills, which detach easily and carry tiny barbs.
Things you shouldn't pet.Cactus: Even fuzzy-looking cacti, like the teddy bear cholla, have barbed spines that cling and hurt.
Things you shouldn't pet.Jellyfish: Some jellyfish can sting even when dead, and washed-up ones on a beach can still hurt.
Things you shouldn't pet.Shark: Most sharks aren't dangerous, but their skin feels like sandpaper, made of tiny tooth-like scales called denticles.
Things you shouldn't pet.Hornet nest: Hornets defend their nests aggressively and can sting many times, unlike a honeybee.
Things you shouldn't pet.Lion: A lion's roar can be heard from up to about 8 kilometers away, and a lion is no pet.
Things you shouldn't pet.Grizzly bear: A grizzly can run about 55 kilometers per hour over short distances, quicker than any person.
Things you shouldn't pet.Rattlesnake: Rattlesnakes have heat-sensing pits, and even a newly dead one can still bite by reflex.
Things you shouldn't pet.Scorpion: Scorpions glow blue-green under UV light, a handy way to spot them before one stings you.
Things you shouldn't pet.Electric eel: An electric eel isn't an eel but a knifefish, and it can deliver up to about 600 volts.
Things you shouldn't pet.Crocodile: Saltwater crocodiles have one of the strongest bites of any living animal, over 3,500 pounds of force.
Things you shouldn't pet.Wolverine: The wolverine is a stocky weasel relative, small but ferocious, and known to drive bears off kills.
Things you shouldn't pet.Skunk: Skunks can spray accurately for about three meters, and the smell is notoriously hard to remove.
Things you shouldn't pet.Puppy: Puppies are born deaf and nearly blind, yet they bond with people quickly through touch and smell.
Things you shouldn't pet.Kitten: Kittens can purr when only a few days old, and the vibration helps them find their mother.
Things you shouldn't pet.Bunny: Rabbits usually like being petted on the forehead and cheeks, but many dislike being picked up.
Things you shouldn't pet.Golden retriever: Golden retrievers were bred in 19th-century Scotland to fetch waterfowl, hence their famously soft mouths.
Things you shouldn't pet.Guinea pig: Guinea pigs are neither pigs nor from Guinea; they're rodents from the Andes in South America.
Things you shouldn't pet.Hamster: Hamsters are nocturnal, so petting a sleeping one in the daytime can startle it into biting.
Things you shouldn't pet.Pony: A pony is a small horse, not a baby horse, and most are under about 14.2 hands tall.
Things you shouldn't pet.Lamb: Lambs can recognize their mother's bleat within days of birth, and they're gentle with people.
Things you shouldn't pet.Labrador: Labradors rank among the most popular dog breeds in many countries, and they're famously patient with kids.
Things you shouldn't pet.Goat: Goats have rectangular pupils, which gives them wide-angle vision.
Things you shouldn't pet.Calf: Calves are social and form bonds, and studies suggest they can recognize individual humans.

Jobs in a restaurant.Chef: The word means chief in French. The tall white hat, the toque, traditionally has about 100 pleats, said to stand for ways to cook an egg.
Jobs in a restaurant.Waiter: Waiters in many countries earn most of their pay through tips, which is why tipping customs differ so widely around the world.
Jobs in a restaurant.Sommelier: A sommelier is a wine expert who advises diners on pairings, and the top level, Master Sommelier, passes one of the hardest exams in food.
Jobs in a restaurant.Host: The host manages the door and seating chart, and good ones plan table turns so the kitchen never gets hit by every order at once.
Jobs in a restaurant.Busser: Bussers clear and reset tables so waiters can focus on service, and in many restaurants waiters tip them out from their own earnings.
Jobs in a restaurant.Dishwasher: The hardest-working job in the building: dishwashers keep a kitchen running, and chef Anthony Bourdain began his career as one.
Jobs in a restaurant.Line cook: Line cooks each run a station, such as grill or sauté, and a good one can plate dozens of dishes in a rush without a pause.
Jobs in a restaurant.Bartender: Bartenders do much more than pour; classic cocktail technique, like shaking versus stirring, changes the texture and dilution of a drink.
Jobs in a restaurant.Maître d': The French phrase means master of the house. The maître d' oversees the dining room and guests, and is often the one who remembers regulars.
Jobs in a restaurant.Sous chef: Sous chef means under chef in French; it is the second in command in the kitchen, running the line when the head chef is away.
Jobs in a restaurant.Pastry chef: Pastry chefs work in a separate precise world, since baking is chemistry, and a few grams of flour more can ruin a cake.
Jobs in a restaurant.Bellhop: Bellhops carry luggage in hotels, not restaurants. The name comes from the bell guests once rang to call them.
Jobs in a restaurant.Usher: Ushers seat people at theatres and weddings. Restaurants have hosts for that job, so this one is in the wrong building.
Jobs in a restaurant.Flight attendant: Flight attendants serve food in the sky, but they work on planes, not in a restaurant, and they are also trained for safety and first aid.
Jobs in a restaurant.Lifeguard: Lifeguards watch pools and beaches. It's the one job here that has nothing to do with feeding anyone, and it demands strong swimming skills.
Jobs in a restaurant.Golf caddie: A caddie carries a golfer's clubs and gives advice on the course. Good ones read greens as well as the players do.
Jobs in a restaurant.Croupier: Croupiers run casino games like roulette and blackjack. The French word originally meant the rider sitting behind on a horse.
Jobs in a restaurant.Bank teller: Bank tellers handle deposits and cash at a branch. ATMs have changed the job, yet bank tellers still exist in large numbers.
Jobs in a restaurant.Librarian: Librarians organise and share information. The job has changed with the internet, but it is not part of restaurant service.
Jobs in a restaurant.Lumberjack: Lumberjacks fell trees, a physically brutal job often ranked among the most dangerous in the world, and nothing to do with dining.
Jobs in a restaurant.Chambermaid: Chambermaids clean hotel rooms. The word chamber means bedroom, so it belongs at a hotel and not at a restaurant.
Jobs in a restaurant.Jockey: Jockeys ride racehorses, and many are tiny by necessity: elite flat-race jockeys often weigh around 50 to 55 kilograms.
Jobs in a restaurant.Lighthouse keeper: Lighthouse keepers once tended the lamp and lived at remote towers; automation has made nearly all of them disappear.
Jobs in a restaurant.Midwife: Midwives help women through pregnancy and birth, and they have been in the profession since ancient times, but not in restaurants.

Things a welder uses.Welding mask: Auto-darkening lenses switch from clear to dark in a tiny fraction of a second when the arc strikes.
Things a welder uses.Welding torch: An oxy-acetylene flame burns at around 3,000 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt steel.
Things a welder uses.Welding gloves: Thick leather gauntlets guard against sparks and heat, and arc radiation can sunburn skin through gaps.
Things a welder uses.Filler rod: Metal melted into the joint to fill the gap, and the right alloy matters as much as the technique.
Things a welder uses.Clamp: Holds pieces in place so heat doesn't warp them, because metal moves as it heats and cools.
Things a welder uses.Angle grinder: Used to cut and clean welds, and its spinning disc is a leading cause of workshop injury.
Things a welder uses.Gas cylinder: Shielding gas like argon flows around the weld to keep air out, and cylinders must be secured upright.
Things a welder uses.Leather apron: Leather resists sparks and spatter, while synthetic fabrics can melt onto skin, so welders avoid polyester.
Things a welder uses.Wire brush: Cleans rust, paint and oxide before welding, because dirty metal makes weak welds.
Things a welder uses.Chipping hammer: Knocks off slag, the crusty glass-like layer that forms over some welds, to reveal the bead underneath.
Things a welder uses.Steel-toe boots: Protect from dropped metal, and welders keep trouser legs over the boots so sparks can't slip inside.
Things a welder uses.Whisk: A kitchen tool for beating eggs, not for fusing metal.
Things a welder uses.Thimble: A sewing finger guard dating back to ancient Rome; a welder's glove does the protecting here.
Things a welder uses.Stethoscope: A doctor's listening tool, not a welder's.
Things a welder uses.Easel: A painter's stand, with no place in a welding shop.
Things a welder uses.Paint roller: A decorator's tool; a welder's finish usually comes from a grinder or wire brush.
Things a welder uses.Piping bag: A baker's icing tool, nothing to do with metal.
Things a welder uses.Pinking shears: Cut fabric edges in a zigzag so they won't fray; welders cut metal with a torch or grinder.
Things a welder uses.Lasso: A looped rope for cattle, not part of a welder's kit.
Things a welder uses.Saddle: A horse's seat, and nowhere near a welding bench.
Things a welder uses.Fishing rod: An angler's tool, not a welder's, though 'filler rod' might fool you.
Things a welder uses.Gavel: A judge's mallet, unlike the welder's chipping hammer.
Things a welder uses.Baton: A conductor's stick, not a welder's tool.
Things a welder uses.Rolling pin: A baker's roller for dough, unrelated to metalwork.

UK police ranks.Constable: The basic rank, whose name comes from the Latin comes stabuli, count of the stable; constables hold an ancient office of personal legal powers.
UK police ranks.Sergeant: Sergeants supervise constables and wear three-chevron stripes, and the word comes from the Latin serviens, meaning servant.
UK police ranks.Inspector: The rank above sergeant, and its star-shaped pips on the shoulder tab make it look like an army officer.
UK police ranks.Chief Inspector: It sits between inspector and superintendent, and it wears three pips on the shoulder.
UK police ranks.Superintendent: A senior officer who often commands a division; the crown on the epaulette marks this rank.
UK police ranks.Chief Constable: Outside London, every territorial force is led by a chief constable, who answers to an elected police and crime commissioner.
UK police ranks.Commissioner: The head of the Metropolitan Police is the Commissioner, and the force was founded in 1829 by Sir Robert Peel, hence the nickname bobbies.
UK police ranks.Commander: A rank used in London's Met and the City of London Police, ranking between chief superintendent and deputy assistant commissioner.
UK police ranks.Deputy Commissioner: The second in command of the Met, after the Commissioner himself or herself.
UK police ranks.Admiral: Admiral is a naval rank, the highest class in the Royal Navy, not in the police.
UK police ranks.Colonel: An army officer rank, pronounced like kernel, which comes from an older French spelling.
UK police ranks.Brigadier: The army rank between colonel and major general, and no British police force uses it.
UK police ranks.Corporal: An army rank for junior non-commissioned officers, and the police use constable instead.
UK police ranks.Major: An army officer rank above captain; not used in the British police.
UK police ranks.Ensign: A junior naval officer rank in the US, and formerly a flag-bearing army rank in Britain.
UK police ranks.Midshipman: A trainee naval officer, famous from sea stories such as Hornblower.
UK police ranks.Squadron Leader: A Royal Air Force rank equivalent to major, commanding a squadron of aircraft.
UK police ranks.Bishop: A senior church figure, and a chess piece too, but never a police rank.
UK police ranks.Cardinal: A senior Catholic official who votes in papal elections, not a cop.
UK police ranks.Lieutenant: The word means place-holder in French; in Britain it's a military rank, and police ranks don't use it though American forces do.
UK police ranks.Private: The lowest army rank, and the police have no equivalent title for a beginner, who is a constable.
UK police ranks.Field Marshal: The highest army rank in Britain, awarded rarely, and not used in policing.
UK police ranks.Petty Officer: A Navy non-commissioned rank, roughly like a sergeant but at sea.
UK police ranks.Captain: Used in the army, navy and US police departments, but UK police forces don't use it.

Social media platforms.Facebook: Mark Zuckerberg launched it at Harvard in 2004 as TheFacebook, and it passed three billion monthly users.
Social media platforms.Instagram: It launched in 2010 as a photo app and was sold to Facebook just 18 months later for about a billion dollars.
Social media platforms.TikTok: Owned by China's ByteDance, it exploded worldwide in the late 2010s with short, algorithm-driven videos.
Social media platforms.Twitter: Its first tweet, in 2006, came from co-founder Jack Dorsey, and the platform was renamed X in 2023.
Social media platforms.Snapchat: Launched in 2011 with disappearing photos, it popularized the story format later copied by other apps.
Social media platforms.Reddit: Founded in 2005 and nicknamed the front page of the internet, it's organized into topic communities called subreddits.
Social media platforms.Pinterest: A visual discovery site where users pin images to boards, and it's popular for recipes and home ideas.
Social media platforms.LinkedIn: Launched in 2003, it's a career network, which Microsoft bought in 2016 for about 26 billion dollars.
Social media platforms.Tumblr: A blogging platform launched in 2007 and bought by Yahoo in 2013, then later sold to Automattic.
Social media platforms.Myspace: It was the biggest social network in the world around 2005 to 2008 before Facebook overtook it, and Tom was everyone's first friend.
Social media platforms.Threads: Meta launched this text app in July 2023, and it gained 100 million sign-ups in about five days.
Social media platforms.Bluesky: A decentralized-style network that began inside Twitter as a research project in 2019, before spinning out on its own.
Social media platforms.Mastodon: A free, open-source network split across many independent servers, launched in 2016, and named after an extinct elephant relative.
Social media platforms.Netflix: Netflix is a streaming service rather than a social network, though people talk about shows on social media all the time.
Social media platforms.Spotify: A music streaming service that has social features such as shared playlists, but not a social network.
Social media platforms.Amazon: An online store founded as a bookseller in 1994, and famous for going far beyond books.
Social media platforms.eBay: Founded in 1995, it's a marketplace for buying and selling, not a social network.
Social media platforms.Excel: A spreadsheet program that, to be fair, many people spend more time in than on social media.
Social media platforms.Zoom: A video-meeting app that boomed in 2020, though it's a communications tool rather than a feed.
Social media platforms.Dropbox: A file storage service founded in 2007, with sharing features but not a social platform.
Social media platforms.Uber: A ride-hailing app launched in 2009, and it's a service rather than a social network.
Social media platforms.Airbnb: A rental marketplace founded in 2008, where reviews do the social work instead of posts.
Social media platforms.PayPal: An online payments company, and it grew out of a 1998 startup that Elon Musk's X.com later merged with.
Social media platforms.Shazam: A song-identification app that Apple bought in 2018, which listens for a few seconds of music and names it.
