Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Google: Google started in a Menlo Park garage in 1998 and now sits in Mountain View at the Googleplex.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Meta: Facebook's parent is based in Menlo Park; the company changed its name from Facebook to Meta in 2021.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Netflix: Based in Los Gatos, Netflix began in 1997 by mailing DVDs, and streaming only arrived a decade later.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Intel: Intel is based in Santa Clara and was co-founded in 1968 by Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, of Moore's Law.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Nvidia: Nvidia in Santa Clara began with graphics chips for games and became central to AI computing.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Adobe: Adobe is in San Jose, and it was named after Adobe Creek, which ran behind co-founder John Warnock's home.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Cisco: Cisco in San Jose took its name from San Francisco, and its original logo even resembled the Golden Gate Bridge.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Uber: Uber, based in San Francisco, was founded in 2009 as UberCab, a black-car service ordered by app.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Airbnb: Airbnb began in San Francisco in 2007 when its founders rented out air mattresses in their apartment.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Salesforce: Salesforce's San Francisco tower is the tallest building in the city, and the company pioneered cloud software in 1999.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.PayPal: PayPal is in San Jose; its early founders include Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and Max Levchin, nicknamed the PayPal Mafia.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Microsoft: Microsoft is headquartered in Redmond, Washington, not California, though its founders began in Albuquerque.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Amazon: Amazon began in Jeff Bezos's garage in the Seattle area and is still headquartered in Washington state.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Dell: Dell is based in Round Rock, Texas; Michael Dell began building computers in his University of Texas dorm room.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.IBM: IBM is headquartered in Armonk, New York, and is well over a century old, having been founded in 1911.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Samsung: Samsung is South Korean, headquartered in Suwon, and began in 1938 as a trading company selling dried fish.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Sony: Sony is headquartered in Tokyo, and its first product, an electric rice cooker, was a commercial flop.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Nintendo: Nintendo is based in Kyoto, Japan, and started in 1889 as a maker of hanafuda playing cards.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Spotify: Spotify is headquartered in Stockholm, Sweden, although it has major offices in the US.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Texas Instruments: True to its name, TI is based in Dallas, Texas, and one of its engineers co-invented the integrated circuit.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Lenovo: Lenovo is based in Beijing and Morrisville, North Carolina, and bought IBM's PC division in 2005.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Nokia: Nokia is Finnish and began in 1865 as a paper mill; later it dominated mobile phones.
Tech companies headquartered in Californ.Valve: Valve is in Bellevue, Washington, not California, and it's the company behind Steam and Half-Life.

Classic programs that came with Windows.Minesweeper: Many people learned right-click from this logic puzzle, which became a fixture of Windows PCs from the 1990s.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Solitaire: Added in Windows 3.0 in 1990 specifically to teach people to drag and drop with a mouse.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Paint: A descendant of the basic bitmap editor in the earliest Windows, it finally gained layers in 2023.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Notepad: It has shipped with Windows since the 1980s, but only gained tabs in Windows 11 in 2023.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Calculator: Included since the first Windows; its source code was released as open source on GitHub in 2019.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Internet Explorer: Bundled with Windows 95 and retired in June 2022 after 27 years, it was long the butt of browser jokes.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Hearts: Debuted in Windows for Workgroups 3.1, where you could play the card game against others over a network.
Classic programs that came with Windows.FreeCell: Nearly every deal is winnable; of the original 32,000 numbered deals, only #11982 is impossible.
Classic programs that came with Windows.WordPad: A basic word processor bundled since Windows 95; Microsoft announced it would be removed in recent Windows 11 versions.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Windows Media Player: Its swirling music visualizations entertained a generation of PC users, who also used it to rip CDs.
Classic programs that came with Windows.3D Pinball: Better known as Space Cadet Pinball, it was a Windows 95 Plus! pack extra and later bundled up to Windows XP.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Movie Maker: Debuted with Windows Me in 2000 and was discontinued in 2017, after an era of home movie editing.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Excel: Part of the Microsoft Office suite, which was sold separately and never bundled with Windows.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Word: Another Office program; the free built-in alternative was WordPad.
Classic programs that came with Windows.PowerPoint: Originally called Presenter, it was bought by Microsoft in 1987 for about $14 million.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Photoshop: Adobe's image editor, created by brothers Thomas and John Knoll; it was never bundled with Windows.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Tetris: Soviet engineer Alexey Pajitnov made it in 1984, and it never shipped with Windows.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Oregon Trail: An educational game from school computers of the 1970s, not a Windows extra.
Classic programs that came with Windows.SimCity: Will Wright's 1989 city builder from Maxis, which was sold separately.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Netscape: Netscape's browser competed with Internet Explorer and lost the browser wars of the 1990s.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Winamp: Nullsoft's 1997 MP3 player, whose startup jingle declared that it really whips the llama's...
Classic programs that came with Windows.iTunes: Apple's software, though Windows users could get it from 2003 onward.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Clippy: Clippy was the Office Assistant in Microsoft Office 97, not Windows itself; its real name was Clippit.
Classic programs that came with Windows.Doom: Microsoft ported Doom to Windows 95 in 1995 as a showcase for gaming, but never bundled it.

VR and AR headsets.Oculus Rift: Palmer Luckey's Kickstarter raised about $2.4 million in 2012, and Facebook bought Oculus for $2 billion in 2014.
VR and AR headsets.Meta Quest: A standalone headset line renamed after Facebook became Meta; it needs no PC or console to run games.
VR and AR headsets.HTC Vive: Room-scale VR built with Valve and released in 2016, which let players physically walk around a play space.
VR and AR headsets.Valve Index: Valve's 2019 headset, known for its high-quality displays and controllers that track each finger individually.
VR and AR headsets.PlayStation VR: Sony's 2016 headset for the PlayStation 4, which became one of the best-selling VR devices of its generation.
VR and AR headsets.Vision Pro: Apple's 2024 headset, which it markets as a spatial computer controlled by eyes, hands and voice.
VR and AR headsets.HoloLens: Microsoft's 2016 augmented reality headset, used by surgeons, engineers and the US military, not just gamers.
VR and AR headsets.Google Cardboard: A 2014 Google design from foldable cardboard that turned a phone into a VR viewer for just a few dollars.
VR and AR headsets.Magic Leap: A Florida startup that raised billions of dollars for augmented reality glasses and headsets.
VR and AR headsets.Gear VR: A headset Samsung made with Oculus in 2015, powered entirely by a Galaxy phone slotted into the front.
VR and AR headsets.Apple Watch: A trap: it's a smartwatch worn on the wrist, so it isn't a headset, though Apple's Vision Pro is.
VR and AR headsets.AirPods: A trap: Apple's wireless earbuds go in your ears, but they don't show virtual worlds.
VR and AR headsets.Fitbit: A trap: it's a wrist fitness tracker, and Google bought the company in 2021, but it's no headset.
VR and AR headsets.Kinect: A trap: Microsoft's motion-sensing camera tracked your body without any headset, in the Xbox era.
VR and AR headsets.Wii Remote: A trap: it's Nintendo's motion controller, which gave a taste of motion gaming, with no headset.
VR and AR headsets.Power Glove: A trap: a 1989 Nintendo glove that looked futuristic, but it was a hand controller and not a headset.
VR and AR headsets.Steam Deck: A trap: Valve's 2022 handheld PC for games, which is not a headset, though Valve also made the Index.
VR and AR headsets.GoPro: A trap: an action camera strapped to helmets and chests that records video, but it's not a headset.
VR and AR headsets.Chromecast: A trap: a streaming dongle from Google that plugs into a TV and casts content, not a headset.
VR and AR headsets.Echo Show: A trap: Amazon's Alexa smart display is a home gadget with a screen, not a wearable headset.
VR and AR headsets.PSP: A trap: Sony's 2004 handheld console was a rival to the Nintendo DS, not a headset.
VR and AR headsets.Game Boy: A trap: a 1989 handheld; Nintendo's Virtual Boy was the real flop in 1995, a red-tinted 3D console.
VR and AR headsets.Nintendo DS: A trap: a dual-screen Nintendo handheld from 2004, which isn't a headset.
VR and AR headsets.Roku: A trap: a streaming player that plugs into your TV, not a headset.

Database systems.MySQL: Named after co-founder Monty Widenius's daughter My, it powers a huge share of the web's sites.
Database systems.PostgreSQL: It descends from the Postgres project at UC Berkeley, and is loved for strict standards and extensibility.
Database systems.MongoDB: Its name comes from humongous; it stores flexible JSON-like documents instead of rigid tables.
Database systems.SQLite: A serverless database in a single file, it is probably the most widely deployed database, living inside phones and browsers.
Database systems.Redis: It keeps data in memory for speed, and its name stands for Remote Dictionary Server.
Database systems.Cassandra: Created at Facebook and named for the Greek prophetess nobody believed, it spreads data across many machines.
Database systems.MariaDB: A fork of MySQL, named after Monty Widenius's younger daughter Maria.
Database systems.DynamoDB: Amazon's managed key-value database, inspired by the Dynamo paper the company published in 2007.
Database systems.Microsoft Access: A desktop database that has shipped with Microsoft Office since the 1990s and let non-programmers build their own apps.
Database systems.Neo4j: A graph database that stores relationships directly, which makes it good at finding connections in social networks.
Database systems.Oracle Database: Larry Ellison's company took its name from a CIA project code-named Oracle that he'd worked on.
Database systems.Python: A programming language, not a database; it often talks to databases through libraries.
Database systems.Java: A programming language; databases are often accessed from it through JDBC.
Database systems.React: A JavaScript UI library from Facebook, not a database.
Database systems.Linux: An operating system kernel that Linus Torvalds began in 1991; many databases run on it.
Database systems.Docker: A container tool, not a database, though databases are often run in its containers.
Database systems.Kubernetes: Google-born container orchestrator whose name is Greek for helmsman; it manages apps, not data.
Database systems.Git: Linus Torvalds wrote it in 2005 to track code, and it's a version control system, not a database.
Database systems.GitHub: A code hosting platform acquired by Microsoft in 2018.
Database systems.Jenkins: An automation server for building and testing code, forked from Hudson.
Database systems.Nginx: A web server pronounced engine-x, created by Igor Sysoev to handle huge numbers of connections.
Database systems.Chrome: Google's browser, launched in 2008, not a database.
Database systems.Node.js: Ryan Dahl released it in 2009 so JavaScript could run on servers; it isn't a database.
Database systems.Photoshop: Adobe's image editor, whose first version was created by Thomas and John Knoll; no database here.

Starter Pokémon from the main games.Bulbasaur: Pokédex number 001, the Grass starter of Red and Blue, carries a seed on its back that grows with it.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Charmander: Its tail flame signals its health and life force, and it evolves into Charizard.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Squirtle: A Water starter in the first games, it inspired the anime's Squirtle Squad.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Chikorita: Gen 2's Grass starter, with a leaf on its head, released with Gold and Silver in 1999.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Cyndaquil: Gen 2's Fire starter is a shy, fire-breathing quill mouse that becomes Typhlosion.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Totodile: A Water starter from Gen 2, a crocodile known for its biting habit.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Treecko: Gen 3's Grass starter, a gecko that evolves into Sceptile.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Torchic: Gen 3's Fire starter chick, evolving into Blaziken, a fighting-type fan favorite.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Mudkip: Gen 3's Water starter became an internet meme in the 2000s.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Turtwig: Gen 4's Grass starter, with a tree growing from its shell.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Chimchar: Gen 4's Fire starter is a monkey with a flame on its tail that becomes the Fire-Fighting Infernape.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Piplup: Gen 4's Water starter, a proud penguin that evolves into Empoleon.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Rowlet: Gen 7's Grass starter, an owl that evolves into Decidueye and can turn its head almost fully around.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Sprigatito: Gen 9's Grass starter, a kitten with a sprout on its head, the face of Scarlet and Violet.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Jigglypuff: A Normal and Fairy singer whose lullaby puts foes to sleep, but never a starter.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Meowth: Team Rocket's talking cat in the anime isn't a starter in any main game.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Psyduck: This headache-plagued Water duck is never a starter.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Snorlax: It sleeps in the road in Gen 1, and you wake it with a Poke Flute; it isn't a starter.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Gengar: A Ghost Pokémon that evolves via trade; never offered as a starter.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Mewtwo: A genetically engineered legendary, not a starter.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Magikarp: A famously useless fish that becomes Gyarados; you buy it, not choose it.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Onix: A Rock giant snake, famous as the Pewter City gym's Pokemon; not a starter.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Lucario: A Fighting and Steel Pokemon introduced in Gen 4 that senses aura; it's not a starter.
Starter Pokémon from the main games.Togepi: It hatches from an egg, and appears as a gift in Gen 2, not as a starter.

Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Mr. Toad: The boastful, car-mad squire of Toad Hall is jailed for stealing a motor car, and Kenneth Grahame based him on the pompous types he knew.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Mole: The timid, home-loving hero abandons his spring cleaning on page one and discovers the river and a new friend.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Ratty: Though called a Water Rat, he is really a water vole, and he famously tells Mole that there is nothing half so worth doing as messing about in boats.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Badger: The gruff, reclusive owner of a house deep in the Wild Wood helps the others retake Toad Hall.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Otter: The river-bank friend whose young son Portly goes missing is a calm, sociable animal, and his name suggests a character from folk tales.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Portly: Otter's lost son is found asleep by the god Pan in the chapter The Piper at the Gates of Dawn, whose title was borrowed for Pink Floyd's first album.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Weasels: The Wild Wooders, who take over Toad Hall while Toad is away, are the book's sneaky, scheming villains.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Stoats: Along with weasels, these sinister Wild Wooders occupy Toad Hall and are driven out by Toad and his friends.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Ferrets: Another gang of Wild Wood invaders in Toad Hall, small, quick and sly.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Winnie-the-Pooh: Milne's honey-loving bear lives in the Hundred Acre Wood, not by Grahame's river.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Piglet: Pooh's timid friend is from Milne's 1926 book, not Wind in the Willows.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Eeyore: The gloomy donkey is Milne's creation, a very different sort of friend to Toad.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Peter Rabbit: Potter's naughty rabbit is not in Grahame's riverbank world; his adventures happen in Mr. McGregor's garden.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle: Beatrix Potter's hedgehog washerwoman is a Potter tale, not a Grahame one.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Paddington: Michael Bond's bear arrived in 1958 from Peru and is a Londoner, not a riverbank animal.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Fantastic Mr Fox: Roald Dahl's clever fox outwits three farmers; it's Dahl's, not Grahame's.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Stuart Little: E. B. White's tiny hero is a New York mouse, not a riverbank character.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Reepicheep: C. S. Lewis's valiant talking mouse sails the Dawn Treader in Narnia, and not along Grahame's river.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Brer Rabbit: The trickster rabbit of Joel Chandler Harris's Uncle Remus tales comes from African American folklore.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Wilbur: E. B. White's pig lives on a farm, not on the riverbank.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Babar: Jean de Brunhoff's elephant king lives in Celesteville.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Hedwig: Harry Potter's snowy owl is a pet, not a Grahame character.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Tigger: Milne's bouncy tiger belongs in the Hundred Acre Wood.
Characters in The Wind in the Willows.Fiver: The nervous, prophetic rabbit of Watership Down is from Richard Adams's 1972 novel.

Genres of fiction.Mystery: Agatha Christie, queen of the genre, remains the best-selling novelist of all time, with around two billion copies sold.
Genres of fiction.Romance: One of the best-selling fiction genres, and its guaranteed happy ending is a defining rule of the form.
Genres of fiction.Fantasy: Tolkien's The Hobbit (1937) helped shape the modern genre, and the word comes from Greek for "making visible".
Genres of fiction.Science fiction: Hugo Gernsback pushed the name in the 1920s, and the Hugo Awards are named after him today.
Genres of fiction.Horror: Frankenstein (1818) is often called both the first sci-fi and the first modern horror novel.
Genres of fiction.Thriller: John Buchan's The Thirty-Nine Steps (1915) is an early template for the fast, tense, chase-driven plot.
Genres of fiction.Western: Rooted in dime novels about the American frontier, Zane Grey sold millions of Westerns in the early 1900s.
Genres of fiction.Historical fiction: Walter Scott's Waverley (1814) is often named the first example, set sixty years before it was written.
Genres of fiction.Dystopian: Orwell's 1984 and Huxley's Brave New World, with a name meaning "bad place", set against More's utopia.
Genres of fiction.Gothic: Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764) launched it, and it's named after medieval architecture.
Genres of fiction.Magical realism: Gabriel Garcia Marquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude mixes the supernatural into ordinary life, as if it were normal.
Genres of fiction.Noir: French for "black", it's hardboiled crime as in Chandler, and French critics coined "film noir".
Genres of fiction.Biography: True-life stories are nonfiction, such as Boswell's Life of Johnson (1791), so they're not fiction genres.
Genres of fiction.Memoir: An author's own recollection of their life, which makes it nonfiction, even when it reads like a novel.
Genres of fiction.Encyclopedia: Diderot's 18th-century French one was a vast Enlightenment project, and it's reference, not fiction.
Genres of fiction.Cookbook: Recipes are nonfiction, and the oldest known European cookbook is a Roman collection attributed to Apicius.
Genres of fiction.Atlas: Named after the Titan, the word was applied to map books by Mercator, and it's nonfiction.
Genres of fiction.Dictionary: Johnson's 1755 dictionary took nine years to write, and a dictionary is reference, not fiction.
Genres of fiction.Almanac: The Old Farmer's Almanac has been published since 1792, and almanacs are nonfiction, full of data and forecasts.
Genres of fiction.Textbook: It teaches a subject, so it's nonfiction, however dull or however gripping you found yours.
Genres of fiction.Thesaurus: Roget published his in 1852, and its name is from Greek for "treasure". It's reference, not fiction.
Genres of fiction.Manual: From Latin "manus", hand, a how-to guide is nonfiction, whatever its instructions feel like.
Genres of fiction.Autobiography: The author's own life story is nonfiction, even when the writer embellishes it as they go.
Genres of fiction.Field guide: Roger Tory Peterson's 1934 bird guide popularized the format, and such guides are nonfiction.

Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Anne Shirley: Anne spells her name with an 'e', and Lucy Maud Montgomery's red-haired orphan from Prince Edward Island makes imagination her superpower.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Marilla Cuthbert: Marilla, stern but secretly soft, expected a boy orphan to help on the farm, and ends up raising Anne instead.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Matthew Cuthbert: Shy Matthew Cuthbert is the one who wants to keep Anne right away, and his death shapes the later chapters.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Diana Barry: Diana Barry is Anne's 'bosom friend', whom she accidentally gets tipsy on what she thought was raspberry cordial.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Gilbert Blythe: Gilbert Blythe calls Anne 'Carrots', and she smashes a slate over his head; the two become rivals and later marry.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Rachel Lynde: Mrs. Rachel Lynde, the village busybody, is the first to comment on Anne's looks and red hair, and has an opinion on everything.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Josie Pye: Josie Pye is Anne's snobbish classmate, who never has a kind word, and whom Anne never quite likes.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Miss Stacy: Miss Stacy is the teacher who encourages Anne's writing and sends her toward the Queen's Academy exam.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Ruby Gillis: Ruby Gillis is Anne's pretty, flirtatious classmate, and her early death in the later books marks the end of childhood.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Mrs. Allan: Mrs. Allan, the minister's wife, becomes Anne's model of a kind, gentle grown-up and teaches her more than the Sunday school.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Jo March: Jo March belongs in Little Women, where Louisa May Alcott's writer heroine lives in Massachusetts, not in Avonlea.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Laurie: Laurie is Jo's wealthy neighbor in Little Women, a rare friend in that novel and unrelated to Prince Edward Island.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Beth March: Beth March is the shy, musical sister in Little Women who dies after scarlet fever, and she's not in Avonlea.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Heidi: Heidi is Johanna Spyri's Swiss orphan who goes to live with her grandfather in the Alps, far from Avonlea.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Pollyanna: Pollyanna plays the 'glad game' in Eleanor Porter's American novel, finding something to be glad about in everything.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Mary Lennox: Mary Lennox is the sour orphan of Frances Hodgson Burnett's The Secret Garden, a different orphan altogether.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Laura Ingalls: Laura Ingalls is the pioneer girl of the Little House books, set on the American prairie.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Sara Crewe: Sara Crewe is the boarding-school heroine of Burnett's A Little Princess, another orphan story but not this one.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Jane Eyre: Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre is a governess in Yorkshire, an orphan like Anne but from a different novel and century.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Elizabeth Bennet: Elizabeth Bennet is the sharp-witted heroine of Austen's Pride and Prejudice, and there are no Bennets in Avonlea.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Scout Finch: Scout Finch narrates To Kill a Mockingbird in Alabama, many miles from Prince Edward Island.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Dorothy Gale: Dorothy Gale is the Kansas girl who is whisked to Oz by a tornado, not to Prince Edward Island.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Miss Honey: Miss Honey is Matilda's gentle teacher in Roald Dahl's novel, and she isn't a character in Avonlea.
Characters in Anne of Green Gables.Peter Pan: Peter Pan is the boy who wouldn't grow up, and Barrie's Neverland is a long way from Green Gables.

Things that melt in the summer sun.Ice cube: An ice cube melts at 0 degrees Celsius, though salt or pressure can change that, and the cracks that form often come from trapped air.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Butter: Butter melts at around 32 to 35 degrees Celsius, which is below body temperature, giving it that smooth feel on the tongue.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Chocolate bar: Cocoa butter melts at about body temperature, which is why chocolate melts in your mouth, and in your hot car.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Ice cream: Ice cream is about half air by volume, and the melted version is a very different mix.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Popsicle: An 11-year-old, Frank Epperson, accidentally invented the Popsicle in 1905 by leaving soda and a stirring stick outside overnight.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Snowman: A snowman is a seasonal sculpture, and one in the sun can lose its shape within hours.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Icicle: Icicles form where meltwater runs and refreezes, so they need both warmth during the day and a freeze afterward.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Snow cone: Shaved ice with syrup is a drink-and-dessert hybrid that begins to melt almost the moment it is served.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Frozen yogurt: Frozen yogurt has a lower fat content than most ice cream, but it melts much the same way in the heat.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Rock: Rock needs well over 600 degrees Celsius to melt, far hotter than any summer day.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Glass bottle: Glass softens only at roughly 600 degrees Celsius or more, so the sun cannot melt it.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Steel spoon: Steel melts at around 1,400 degrees Celsius, so a spoon stays solid in any heat wave.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Brick: Bricks are fired in kilns at over 900 degrees Celsius, so a summer sun cannot melt them.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Sand: Sand only melts above 1,700 degrees Celsius, and when it does, it becomes glass.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Seashell: Seashells are made of calcium carbonate, which does not melt in the sun, but it does dissolve in acid.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Wooden bench: Wood doesn't melt; it chars and burns instead, because heat breaks down its cellulose first.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Ceramic mug: Ceramic is fired at over 1,000 degrees Celsius, so sunshine cannot melt it.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Paper: Paper does not melt, but burns at about 233 degrees Celsius, a temperature Ray Bradbury turned into a title.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Bread: Bread doesn't melt; heat just dries it out into toast-like crusts and, left long enough, stale slices.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Banana: A banana turns soft and brown in the sun, but it rots rather than melts.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Apple: An apple left in the sun softens as it spoils, but it never melts into a liquid.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Pretzel: A pretzel is baked solid, and the sun will only make it stale, not melt it.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Cotton shirt: Cotton does not melt at all; it scorches before it would turn to liquid, unlike polyester, which can melt.
Things that melt in the summer sun.Penny: A modern US penny is zinc with a thin copper coat, and it melts at over 400 degrees, so the sun cannot touch it.

Things that are hollow.Drinking straw: The first paper straws were wax-coated tubes made by Marvin Stone in 1888, who rolled paper around a pencil.
Things that are hollow.Pipe: A pipe is hollow tube, and Roman engineers laid lead ones; the word 'plumbing' comes from Latin plumbum, lead.
Things that are hollow.Flute: The oldest known musical instruments are flutes made from bird bone, found in German caves and about 40,000 years old.
Things that are hollow.Basketball: A basketball is hollow, filled with air at about 8 psi, and has bounced since the first game in 1891.
Things that are hollow.Garden hose: Hoses are hollow tubes, and the first known flexible ones were made of leather in the 1600s by Dutch firefighters.
Things that are hollow.Drum: A drum's hollow body resonates, and this is why bigger drums have deeper tones.
Things that are hollow.Balloon: A balloon is hollow, and when it bursts the rubber snaps back, which is why it makes that loud bang.
Things that are hollow.Bell: A bell is hollow so it can ring, and the bronze alloy has been the standard for thousands of years.
Things that are hollow.Ping-pong ball: A table tennis ball is a hollow plastic shell just 2.7 grams in weight, which is why it bounces so lively.
Things that are hollow.Bamboo: Bamboo is a hollow grass, and it can grow up to a meter a day in some species.
Things that are hollow.Tunnel: A tunnel is hollow by definition, and the Gotthard Base Tunnel in Switzerland is the world's longest at about 57 kilometers.
Things that are hollow.Bottle: A bottle is hollow, and ancient Egyptian glassmakers made the first ones around 1500 BC.
Things that are hollow.Brick: Most bricks are solid, but modern ones often have holes to lighten them.
Things that are hollow.Marble: Marbles are solid glass, so they are not hollow.
Things that are hollow.Golf ball: Modern golf balls have a solid or layered core, not a hollow one, and old ones had a feather-stuffed leather cover.
Things that are hollow.Pencil: A pencil's graphite core is solid, wrapped in wood, which is why it's not hollow.
Things that are hollow.Bowling ball: Bowling balls are solid with finger holes, and the core determines how they hook.
Things that are hollow.Rock: A rock is solid, though some rocks like geodes have hollow crystal-lined centers.
Things that are hollow.Billiard ball: Billiard balls are solid, historically made of ivory and now of plastic resin.
Things that are hollow.Baseball: A baseball is not hollow, but wound with yarn around a cork and rubber core.
Things that are hollow.Carrot: Carrots are solid roots, so no hollow inside.
Things that are hollow.Candle: A candle is solid wax around a wick, and it melts as it burns.
Things that are hollow.Crayon: A crayon is solid colored wax, and the first Crayola box in 1903 had eight colors.
Things that are hollow.Coin: A coin is solid metal, unlike hollow chocolate coins.

Things made of glass.Wine glass: A wet finger circling the rim of a wine glass can make it sing because the glass vibrates at its natural frequency.
Things made of glass.Light bulb: Edison didn't invent the light bulb but made a practical one, and it was the glass vacuum that kept the filament from burning up.
Things made of glass.Test tube: Test tubes are often made of borosilicate glass, which resists sudden heat changes far better than ordinary glass.
Things made of glass.Fishbowl: Goldfish in a small round bowl struggle because little water holds less oxygen, which is why experts advise larger tanks.
Things made of glass.Mason jar: Named after John Landis Mason, who patented the screw-top jar in 1858, it let families preserve food through winter.
Things made of glass.Windshield: A car windshield is laminated glass: two sheets with a plastic layer, so it cracks but holds together on impact.
Things made of glass.Beer bottle: Beer bottles are often brown because the dark glass blocks UV light that would otherwise spoil the hops flavour.
Things made of glass.Hourglass: Sand in an hourglass flows at a nearly constant rate, no matter how full the top bulb is, which is why it works as a timer.
Things made of glass.Stained glass: The vivid colours come from metal oxides mixed into the molten glass, such as gold for red and cobalt for blue.
Things made of glass.Mirror: Modern mirrors are glass backed with a thin layer of silver or aluminium, and the glass just protects the metal.
Things made of glass.Lab beaker: Lab beakers are usually borosilicate glass, often sold under the brand name Pyrex, because it survives heating well.
Things made of glass.Soda can: It is made of aluminium, and recycling one saves about 95 percent of the energy needed to make a new one.
Things made of glass.Milk carton: It is coated paperboard, and the wax or plastic coating is what keeps it from going soggy.
Things made of glass.Water balloon: It is latex, which is natural rubber that stretches several times its size before popping.
Things made of glass.Rubber boot: Rubber boots are waterproof because rubber is, and natural rubber was used by Amazon peoples long before industry.
Things made of glass.Frisbee: It is moulded plastic, and the toy was inspired by pie tins from the Frisbie Baking Company, which students tossed around.
Things made of glass.Plastic straw: Plastic straws are a polypropylene product, and they have been banned in many places since the 2010s.
Things made of glass.Tin can: Most "tin" cans are really steel coated with a thin layer of tin to prevent rust, so no glass is involved.
Things made of glass.Paper cup: Paper cups have a thin plastic lining, which makes them hard to recycle despite looking like paper.
Things made of glass.Wine cork: Cork is the bark of a tree, so it is the stopper for a glass bottle but not made of glass.
Things made of glass.Terracotta pot: Terracotta means "baked earth" in Italian, and the porous clay lets moisture pass through the walls, unlike glass.
Things made of glass.Car tire: A tire is rubber over steel and fabric cords, with carbon black that gives it its colour and wear resistance.
Things made of glass.Brick: Bricks are fired clay, among the oldest building materials, and some sun-dried ones date back over 9,000 years.
Things made of glass.Ceramic mug: A ceramic mug is fired clay with a glassy glaze, so it looks glassy but is a different material.

Famous bridges.Golden Gate Bridge: Its famous color is 'International Orange', chosen to stand out in San Francisco's fog, and it was the longest suspension span when opened in 1937.
Famous bridges.Brooklyn Bridge: Opened in 1883, it was the world's longest suspension bridge, and its builder John Roebling died of tetanus during preparation.
Famous bridges.Tower Bridge: Often mistaken for London Bridge, this Victorian bascule bridge opened in 1894 and its upper walkways were once used by pickpockets.
Famous bridges.Rialto Bridge: The oldest bridge across Venice's Grand Canal, rebuilt in stone in 1591, and it's lined with shops.
Famous bridges.Ponte Vecchio: Florence's medieval bridge is lined with jewelers' shops, and it was the only one the Germans spared in WWII.
Famous bridges.Charles Bridge: A 14th-century stone bridge in Prague with 30 statues, and legend says builders mixed eggs into the mortar.
Famous bridges.Millau Viaduct: In southern France, its tallest mast reaches higher than the Eiffel Tower, making it the tallest bridge in the world.
Famous bridges.Bridge of Sighs: Venice's covered bridge linked the courtroom to the prison, and the name comes from prisoners sighing at a last view of the city.
Famous bridges.Forth Bridge: The red cantilever railway bridge near Edinburgh opened in 1890, and 'painting the Forth Bridge' became a phrase for an endless task.
Famous bridges.Harbour Bridge: Sydney's steel arch bridge opened in 1932, and people have climbed it for tourism since 1998, earning the nickname 'the Coathanger'.
Famous bridges.Pont Neuf: The name means 'new bridge', but it's the oldest standing bridge across the Seine in Paris, completed in 1607.
Famous bridges.Hoover Dam: It's a dam on the Colorado River, not a bridge, though a bypass bridge nearby carries traffic.
Famous bridges.Channel Tunnel: A rail tunnel beneath the English Channel, about 50 km long, and no bridge in it.
Famous bridges.Panama Canal: A waterway that cuts across Panama, and a canal, not a bridge, though the Bridge of the Americas crosses it.
Famous bridges.Suez Canal: A canal linking the Mediterranean and Red seas, where bridges cross, but it isn't a bridge.
Famous bridges.Three Gorges Dam: The world's largest power station by capacity, in China, and a dam, not a bridge.
Famous bridges.Great Wall: China's long series of defences isn't a bridge, though it crosses many valleys.
Famous bridges.Hadrian's Wall: A Roman frontier across northern Britain built from AD 122, not a bridge.
Famous bridges.London Eye: A giant observation wheel on the Thames, not a bridge, though close to several.
Famous bridges.CN Tower: A Toronto tower that was the tallest freestanding structure in the world until 2007, not a bridge.
Famous bridges.Gateway Arch: St. Louis's arch is a monument rather than a bridge, though it overlooks the Mississippi.
Famous bridges.Arc de Triomphe: A Paris victory monument, and not a bridge, though it's an arch.
Famous bridges.Hollywood Sign: A hillside sign in Los Angeles, not a bridge.
Famous bridges.Big Ben: A bell, in London's clock tower, and not a bridge, though it's beside Westminster Bridge.

Words you'd see on road signs.Stop: The octagon is unique to stop signs, so drivers recognize one even from behind or when it is covered in snow.
Words you'd see on road signs.Yield: Yield signs are inverted triangles, a shape used for no other sign, so drivers know it from afar.
Words you'd see on road signs.Give Way: Give Way means the same as Yield and is used in Britain, Ireland and Australia, though many countries use only a symbol.
Words you'd see on road signs.One Way: One Way signs point where traffic is allowed to flow, and one-way streets help traffic move faster and avoid head-on crashes.
Words you'd see on road signs.Detour: Detour comes from the French 'détour', 'a turning aside', and signs often use orange to catch attention.
Words you'd see on road signs.Slow: A 'Slow' sign is a simple word warning, and many countries prefer pictograms, which tourists and non-readers also understand.
Words you'd see on road signs.Merge: Traffic engineers recommend the 'zipper merge': use both lanes until the merge point, then alternate, which keeps traffic flowing.
Words you'd see on road signs.Speed Limit: In 1896, Walter Arnold became Britain's first speeder, caught doing 8 mph in a 2 mph zone, after his car was chased down by a policeman on a bicycle.
Words you'd see on road signs.Dead End: A cul-de-sac literally means 'bottom of the sack' in French, which is the origin of the dead-end street.
Words you'd see on road signs.Road Works: US construction signs are orange because that color catches the eye and signals temporary danger.
Words you'd see on road signs.No U-turn: The No U-turn symbol crosses out a U-shaped arrow, and the turn is banned because it cuts across the opposing lanes.
Words you'd see on road signs.Fragile: Fragile labels go on parcels, not road signs, and they ask handlers to take extra care.
Words you'd see on road signs.Push: Push is for doors, and a road sign wouldn't tell you to push anything.
Words you'd see on road signs.Pull: Pull is for doors, so it is not a road instruction.
Words you'd see on road signs.Wet Paint: Wet Paint signs warn pedestrians of fresh paint, and they are for walls and benches, not roads.
Words you'd see on road signs.This Way Up: This Way Up is for packages, and its arrows tell handlers how to keep the contents upright.
Words you'd see on road signs.Sale: Sale signs hang in shop windows, and no road authority would put one on a highway.
Words you'd see on road signs.Vacancy: Vacancy signs belong to hotels and motels, and they flash neon along roadsides.
Words you'd see on road signs.Encore: Encore means 'again' in French, and audiences shout it at concerts, not at road signs.
Words you'd see on road signs.Checkmate: Checkmate comes from the Persian 'shah mat', 'the king is helpless', and belongs to chess.
Words you'd see on road signs.Gift Shop: Gift Shop signs welcome visitors at museums and attractions, but they are not road regulations.
Words you'd see on road signs.Fasten Seatbelts: Roads say 'Buckle Up'. 'Fasten Seatbelts' is the sign you see on an airplane.
Words you'd see on road signs.Do Not Disturb: Do Not Disturb hangs on hotel doorknobs, and it isn't a road rule.
Words you'd see on road signs.Keep Off the Grass: Keep Off the Grass is for parks and lawns, and a road sign wouldn't need it.

Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Elevator: Elisha Otis demonstrated his safety brake in 1854 by cutting the rope while standing on a lift, which made tall buildings possible.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Lobby: A skyscraper lobby is often a showpiece; the word lobby, in its political sense, came from the hall where lawmakers were approached.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Penthouse: The word originally meant a sloping lean-to roof, but now it means a luxury apartment at the top of a building.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Observation deck: The deck on the Empire State Building has welcomed millions of visitors since 1931, and the Burj Khalifa's is on its 124th floor.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Revolving door: Invented in 1888, revolving doors reduce drafts, saving energy and helping stop wind from blowing through tall buildings.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Stairwell: Skyscrapers need enclosed fire-resistant stairwells, since lifts are not used in a fire; some climb them in races.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Security desk: Most office towers have a front desk that checks visitors and badges, which is far more common than the Hollywood heists suggest.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Window cleaner: Window cleaners in tall towers work from suspended platforms, and some buildings use robotic cleaning rigs.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Escalator: Escalators were first shown at the 1900 Paris Exposition, and the name started as a trademark of the Otis company.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Hayloft: A trap: a hayloft is the upper level of a barn where hay is stored, a feature of farms, not skyscrapers.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Moat: A moat is a defensive ditch around a castle, filled with water, not a skyscraper feature.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Dungeon: A dungeon was a castle's prison, often underground. Skyscrapers have basements and parking garages instead.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Thatched roof: Thatch is dried straw or reed, a roofing for cottages, but it is not fireproof enough for skyscrapers.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Paddock: A paddock is a small enclosed field for horses, and would not appear in a skyscraper.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Drawbridge: A drawbridge is a castle's raised or lowered bridge, but skyscrapers have lobbies and revolving doors.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Pigsty: A pigsty is a pen for pigs; not a place in the sky, though some vertical farms are now in cities.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Chicken coop: Chicken coops are for hens, and are found in back gardens; even rooftop farms are far from the usual skyscraper feature.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Portcullis: A portcullis is a heavy grille that slides down to block a castle gate, a medieval, not modern, security feature.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Haystack: A haystack is a pile of hay in a field; not a skyscraper feature, but as in 'needle in a haystack'.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Igloo: An igloo is a snow shelter built by Inuit hunters, and is the opposite of a skyscraper in both material and form.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Outhouse: An outhouse is an outdoor toilet, and skyscrapers have indoor plumbing, with water pumped up hundreds of meters.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Water wheel: Water wheels turn with flowing rivers to power mills; a skyscraper would rely on elevators and electricity instead.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Mud hut: Mud huts are built from earth and are common in parts of Africa, a different building from a skyscraper.
Things you'd find in a skyscraper.Well: A well draws groundwater from below, which is the opposite of a tall tower that pumps water up to its top floors.

Things worn on the head.Hat: A hat is the most common head covering; the top hat was invented in the 1790s and is associated with formal wear.
Things worn on the head.Beanie: The beanie probably gets its name from slang for head ('bean'), and it began as a cap worn by college freshmen.
Things worn on the head.Turban: A turban is a long cloth wound round the head, and in Sikhism it's a sacred part of dress.
Things worn on the head.Beret: The beret is the traditional cap of Basque shepherds, and is now strongly associated with French style and military units.
Things worn on the head.Fedora: The fedora is named for an 1882 play, Fedora, in which actress Sarah Bernhardt wore one.
Things worn on the head.Tiara: A tiara is a jeweled semicircular crown for women, and weddings and royals often feature them.
Things worn on the head.Helmet: The Ancient Greeks wore bronze helmets in battle, and today helmets are standard gear in sports like cycling.
Things worn on the head.Sombrero: The Spanish word for 'shade', a sombrero has a wide brim to protect from the Mexican sun.
Things worn on the head.Fez: The fez is named after the Moroccan city of Fez, and it was the official headwear in the Ottoman Empire after 1826.
Things worn on the head.Crown: The Imperial State Crown of the United Kingdom has the Cullinan II diamond, which is about 317 carats.
Things worn on the head.Headband: Headbands keep hair back, and Ancient Greek athletes wore them.
Things worn on the head.Bonnet: A bonnet is a head covering tied under the chin; in British English it is also the hood of a car.
Things worn on the head.Balaclava: This knitted cap, covering the face, is named for the Crimean War battle of Balaclava, where British troops were chilled.
Things worn on the head.Cardigan: A trap: a cardigan covers the body, not the head; it's named for the 7th Earl of Cardigan.
Things worn on the head.Mitten: A mitten covers the hand, with a single section for the fingers, and keeps hands warmer than gloves.
Things worn on the head.Sandal: Sandals are some of the oldest known footwear, and were worn on feet, not heads.
Things worn on the head.Necklace: A necklace goes round the neck, and some of the oldest known jewelry is shell beads, over 100,000 years old.
Things worn on the head.Belt: A belt holds up trousers at the waist, not worn on the head.
Things worn on the head.Apron: An apron protects clothes at the front; the word came from 'a napron', and was reinterpreted over time.
Things worn on the head.Glove: Gloves cover hands and have been used since ancient times; falconers used heavy ones.
Things worn on the head.Sock: Socks go on the feet; the oldest known were knitted in Egypt in about the 11th century.
Things worn on the head.Corset: A corset shapes the torso and was popular for centuries, and is certainly not for the head.
Things worn on the head.Poncho: A poncho hangs from the shoulders, originating in the Andes, and has a hole for the head, but is not worn on it.
Things worn on the head.Cufflink: A cufflink fastens a shirt cuff at the wrist, not a head item.
